questions.stem:
Sam is a telephone sales representative.

For each call to a customer

• Sam either makes a sale or does not make a sale
• sales are made independently

Past records show that, for each call to a customer, the probability that Sam makes a sale is 0.2

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Find the probability that Sam makes
(i) exactly 2 sales in 14 calls,
(ii) more than 3 sales in 25 calls.
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
(i) $X \sim \mathrm{B}(14,0.2)$
$[\mathrm{P}(X=2)=]\ ^{14}C_2 \times 0.2^2 \times 0.8^{12}$ M1
$=0.2501$ awrt 0.2501 A1
(ii) $X \sim \mathrm{B}(25,0.2)$
$\mathrm{P}(X>3)=1-\mathrm{P}(X \leqslant 3)=1-0.2340$ or $1-(0.0038+0.0236+0.0708+0.1358)$ M1
$=0.7660$ awrt 0.766 A1
(a)(i) M1: For writing or using $^{14}C_2 \times 0.2^2 \times 0.8^{12}$ (Allow 91 for $^{14}C_2$)
A1: awrt 0.2501 NB 0.2501 with no working scores M1A1
(ii) M1: For writing or using $1-\mathrm{P}(X \leqslant 3)$
A1: awrt 0.766 NB awrt 0.766 with no working scores M1A1

parts.label: b(i)
parts.text:
Sam makes $n$ calls each day.
(b) Find the minimum value of $n$
(i) so that the expected number of sales each day is at least 6
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
$[np=6 \Rightarrow]\ n = \frac{6}{0.2}$ M1
$=30$ A1
M1: For use of $np=6$ e.g. $0.2n=6$ (Allow $\geqslant$)
A1: Cao

parts.label: b(ii)
parts.text:
(ii) so that the probability of at least 1 sale in a randomly selected day exceeds 0.95
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
$Y \sim \mathrm{B}(n,0.2)$ we require $\mathrm{P}(Y \geqslant 1)>0.95$
$1-\mathrm{P}(Y=0)>0.95 \Rightarrow \mathrm{P}(Y=0)<0.05$ M1
$[^nC_0 \times 0.2^0] \times 0.8^n < 0.05$ M1
$0.8^{14}=0.04398...[<0.05]$ or $n>\frac{\ln 0.05}{\ln 0.8} \Rightarrow n>13.425$ dM1
$n=14$ A1
M1: For writing or using $\mathrm{P}(Y \geqslant 1)=1-\mathrm{P}(Y=0)$ (Allow $\mathrm{P}(Y \geqslant 1)=1-\mathrm{P}(Y \leqslant 0)$)
M1: For $0.8^n<0.05$ oe (Allow = or $\leqslant$)
dM1: Dependant on previous M1. For substitution of n (allow $0.8^{13}=0.05497...$) or rearranging to $n> ...$ (Allow = or $\geqslant$). If using logs allow any base e.g. $n > \log_{0.8} 0.05$
A1: Cao

questions.stem:
The discrete random variable $X$ is given by

$X \sim \mathrm{B}(n,p)$

The value of $n$ and the value of $p$ are such that $X$ can be approximated by a normal random variable $Y$ where

$Y \sim \mathrm{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)$

Given that when using a normal approximation

$\mathrm{P}(X<86)=0.2266$ and $\mathrm{P}(X>97)=0.1056$

parts.label: a
parts.mark_scheme:
$\frac{97.5-\mu}{\sigma}=1.25$ M1 M1
$\frac{85.5-\mu}{\sigma}=-0.75$ M1 M1
M1
$2\sigma=12$ M1
$\sigma=6^*\ [\mu=90]$ dA1*
NB Condone use of $np$ for $\mu$ and $\sqrt{np(1-p)}$ for $\sigma$
M1: For standardising using 96.5/97/97.5 and $=$ z value, where $1<z<1.5$
M1: For standardising using 85.5/86/86.5 and $=$ z value, where $-1<z<-0.5$
M1: For use of a correct continuity correction in either equation
M1: For a correct z value used in either equation
M1: An attempt at both equations with one fully correct
dA1: Dependent on all previous M marks being awarded $\sigma=6^*$ As this is a show that question then working must be seen; For solving simultaneously eliminating $\mu$ or $\sigma$
Official notes (completeness pass):
- M1: For solving simultaneously eliminating $\mu$ or $\sigma$ As this is a show that question then working must be seen.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) Hence find the value of $n$ and the value of $p$
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
$np=90$ and $np(1-p)=36$ M1
$1-p=0.4$ M1
$p=0.6$ and $n=150$ A1
M1: For $np=\mu$ and $np(1-p)=\sigma^2$ Follow through their $\mu$ (Condone $npq=\sigma^2$)
M1: For solving simultaneously. May be implied by a correct value for p and n
A1: Both $p=0.6$ and $n=150$
